title: The Big Episode on Wikipedia
summary: Josh and Chuck explore Wikipedia: the hosts' longstanding show policy of not using it as a source and Chuck's revised view of its reliability. They cover its scale and funding, the pre-history in web directories and webrings, the origins in Bomis and the slow-moving Nupedia (spelled New Pedia in transcript), Ward Cunningham's WikiWikiWeb and Cunningham's law, the Wales-Sanger split and Wikipedia's January 15, 2001 launch, the September 11 attacks article that shaped its culture, Larry Sanger's criticisms, the Wikimedia Foundation and the five pillars, editor conduct rules and blocks/bans, reliability studies and errors, featured and good articles, editor demographics and gender bias, the John Seigenthaler hoax, and tips for editing. The episode closes with a listener mail about bonsai.

segments.title: Opening banter and Chuck's changed view
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, then Chuck says that after researching Wikipedia his view has softened, though the show's no-Wikipedia-source policy stays.

segments.title: What Wikipedia is: stats and funding
segments.summary: Overview of Wikipedia as a large online encyclopedia with about 62 million articles, 300-plus languages, billions of monthly visitors, and edit statistics. It runs without ads on donations, with an operating budget of about 168 million dollars a year.

segments.title: Pre-Wikipedia web directories and webrings
segments.summary: Early web directories such as Yahoo's, and the Bomis webring concept, which was open source and used webmasters to link sites on a topic.

segments.title: Bomis and the origins of Nupedia
segments.summary: Bomis focused on adult content before Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger pursued a free encyclopedia called Nupedia (called New Pedia in the episode). Its seven-step expert review process made it very slow.

segments.title: Ward Cunningham and the first wiki
segments.summary: Ward Cunningham built the first wiki, WikiWikiWeb, named after Hawaii's wiki wiki shuttle buses, initially as a tool for programmers. Cunningham's law says posting a wrong answer gets a quick correction.

segments.title: Wikipedia's founding and the wiki dispute
segments.summary: Nupedia became a wiki after Sanger was introduced to the concept. The dispute over who proposed it is discussed, with Sanger crediting a dinner conversation. Wikipedia launched on January 15, 2001.

segments.title: Early Wikipedia and the September 11 article
segments.summary: Early Wikipedia growth and the September 11, 2001 attacks, when news sites crashed and Wikipedia's article became a main source of information and set the community's norms.

segments.title: Trolls, Sanger's departure and criticism
segments.summary: Trolls and the lack of structure led Sanger to quit after about fourteen months. He became a prominent critic and argued Wikipedia had a left-wing bias, which the hosts question.

segments.title: Wikimedia Foundation and Spanish fork
segments.summary: Spanish Wikipedians objected to ads and created a fork, which led Wales to found the Wikimedia Foundation in 2003 and shut down Nupedia.

segments.title: The five pillars of Wikipedia
segments.summary: The five pillars are described: it is an encyclopedia, it is free, neutrality, editors treat each other with respect and civility, and Wikipedia has no firm rules. Assume good faith is discussed.

segments.title: Editing rules, vandalism and spam
segments.summary: Hosts describe the rules for editors, including vandalism, spamming, the three-revert rule, copyright violations, and sock puppetry.

segments.title: Administrators, blocks and bans
segments.summary: Volunteer administrators decide on blocks, which are temporary and preventative, and on bans, which can be site-wide or global.

segments.title: Is Wikipedia reliable? Errors, featured articles and citogenesis
segments.summary: A 2005 study compared Wikipedia with Britannica, finding slightly more mistakes per article in Wikipedia. Fake facts about dead philosophers were corrected at varying speeds. Good and featured articles are labeled. Wikipedia says it is not a reliable source, and the XKCD cytogenesis example and the Peaking Duck backstage story are described.

segments.title: Editor demographics, gender gap and the Seigenthaler hoax
segments.summary: Most editors are men and most are white, which causes gender bias in biographies. Edit-a-thons are held to address this. The 2005 John Seigenthaler hoax led to criticism, and reputation improved after the 2010s.

segments.title: Getting started editing Wikipedia
segments.summary: Tutorials, the Wikipedia Adventure, the Tea House and help desk are mentioned as ways for new editors to learn how to contribute.

segments.title: Bonsai inspiration listener mail
segments.summary: Listener Nathan Staker and his father Brent write that the show's bonsai episode inspired them to grow thirty trees and join the Utah Bonsai Club.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and remind them how to send mail, then sign off.
